before: The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx [1].
GERD is a gastrointestinal motility disorder that results from the reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity resulting in symptoms or complications [1].
It affects quality of life and may cause erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma [1].
GERD is a clinical diagnosis and is most effectively treated with proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) [1].
Long-term use of PPIs is associated with bone fractures, chronic renal disease, acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection [1].
In children, GER refers to the involuntary passage of gastric contents into the esophagus and is often physiological and managed conservatively [2].
GER disease (GERD) in children is a less common pathologic process causing troublesome symptoms, which may need medical management [2].

Factors that play a role in the pathogenesis of GERD include abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, as well as anatomical defects of the lower esophageal reflux barrier such as hiatal hernia [2].
The clinical manifestations of GERD in young children are varied and nonspecific prompting the necessity for careful diagnostic evaluation [2].
Management should be targeted to the underlying aetiopathogenesis and to limit complications of GERD [2].
Symptoms potentially attributable to gastroesophageal reflux disease are among those most commonly reported to primary care providers in the outpatient setting [3].

Clinical approaches to the evaluation and management of these symptoms include proton pump inhibitor trials as well as specific indications or clinical settings that warrant referral to Gastroenterology specialists [3].
